## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll read games 157 and 156, retain the 20k opponent, and play game 158 to completion. I’ll save the move history and review, focusing on early area counts and viable eye space.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

D8/D9 joined D7 and retained the top endpoint; Black E8 followed.
Black27 C8 cut with B8/C9 liberties and was separate from B7.
White B8 occupied one liberty; Black B6 saved B7 by joining C6/D6.
White30 C9 captured the C8 cutter and joined D9/main.
Capture REOPENED C8 for B8, C7 and D8. B8 was still physically separate from the upper main.

White32 B9 actually joined B8 to C9/main while preserving the true C8 eye.
Black33 A8 then entered the prospective second-eye boundary.
Final upper seven B8/B9/C7/C9/D7/D8/D9 have only A9/C8 liberties.
C8 is a true one-point eye with B8/C7/C9/D8 all in the same chain.
A9 borders opposing A8; it is not a second true eye.
The joining move solved connectivity while leaving the second room's entry open.

Manual unplayed audit after A8:
A7 would atari isolated Black A8 to sole A9, but White A7 itself has sole A6.
Black A6 can join B6 and capture the attacking A7, REOPENING A7 for A8.
Thus the apparently winning edge atari cannot be evaluated without its attacker's own liberties.
A9 first would join the White main and atari A8 to A7, but Black A7 can actually join A8 to B7.
No upper rescue was submitted. These local checks are not an exhaustive proof against every whole-board defense.

A8 before B9 is a relevant manual candidate to examine in a future comparable position:
it would occupy the observed entry and join B8, while C8 stays open.
This was not played, searched or verified as an optimal or forced-winning alternative.
The actionable lesson is to audit the second-eye entry before choosing the connection order.

Upper reference A-D rows8-9 eight +C7/D7 two=10 had already lost A8 after33.
The resulting seven stones+C8 one+A9 mixed one are NOT nine living area.

## Another base competed for the same development turns

White34 G7,36 H7,38 J7 formed an actual upper-right chain.
Black F7/F6 joined E7-E9 to G6/H6; J6 joined H6.
White retained the J7 endpoint but still needed a left/top boundary and two rooms.
An unfinished G/H/J rows7-9 nine-point outline was not territory.

White40 J5 preserved the right main's upper eye boundary.
Black41 G8 then entered the unfinished upper-right base.
G8 stayed separate from the F-file Black chain, with F8/G9/H8 liberties.
Upper White G7/H7/J7 ended with only H8/J8, both in ONE connected mixed-boundary region:
F8/F9/G9/H8/H9/J8/J9.
This was neither two eyes nor unconditional life.
Preserving J5 helped the established right base, but did not automatically preserve the other base.
No forced winning choice between these competing urgencies is established.

## Lower corner and resignation audit

White42 D3 joined the long-neglected C3.
Black D2 took its lower endpoint.
White44 H4 completed right life; Black45 C4 joined D4 and capped the lower-left above.
Final C3/D3 have only B3/C2, no protected eye room.
There was no affordable proven life schedule or credible winning territorial recovery at resignation.
No exhaustive search over all possible defenses or new invasions is claimed.

Final inventories:
White22 stones: upper-left7, upper-right3, right10, lower-left2.
Black22 stones in eight physical chains; do not invent a single connected wall.
Black E5, E3 and D2 remain separate; A8 and G8 also remain separate.
Upper Black E7/E8/E9/F6/F7/G6/H6/J6 is one chain, separate from left B6/B7/C6/D6.
C4/D4 is a pair; F2/G1/G2 is another chain.

Displayed geometric totals, retaining all stones:
Black22+E6 one=23.
White22+C8 one+J4 one+J1/J2 two=26.
Mixed-boundary32: A9 one; upper-right seven; left/lower twenty; E4/F3/F4/F5 four.
23+26+32=81.
These are NOT an official score, settled area totals or a dead-stone assessment.
No manual removal score is offered for a resignation.
Only the right13 has a completed two-room proof in this review.

## Carry forward

Retain20k:26 wins/121 losses/6 draws;87 unfinished/excluded.
Read158/157 before the next game; consult154 for broad continuous development.

- More separate bases demand more endpoint and eye-making turns. C3/C7/G3 left all three unfinished; additional G7 did not cure that cost.
- Count after the cap, not just before development. The live42 reference was not maintained; do not reuse it as owned area.
- H2/H1 before the lower edge closed, then H3's actual join, preserved a usable right room.
- J3/J5/H4 completed independent J1/J2 and J4 rooms: right13. Capture was not needed for this life.
- C9 capture reopened C8; B9 made an actual join but allowed A8 to remove the second eye. Audit entry protection alongside connectivity.
- A7 atari is itself soleA6; A6 captures the attacker and reopens A7. A9 atari permits A7's actual join to B7.
- G7/H7/J7 retained one endpoint, but G8 invaded before the other boundary completed. H8/J8 belong to one mixed region, not two eyes.
- C3 was neglected until42; D2/C4 caps left C3/D3 on B3/C2, no eyes. The secure right13 could not justify a winning count.
- No promotion, opening improvement or optimal-move claim follows; preserve the exact history and uncertainty.
`;

const focus=review.slice(review.indexOf('## Carry forward'));
store('focus',focus);

text(await tools.apply_patch('*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: '+path+'\n+'+value.trimEnd().replace(/\n/g,'\n+')+'\n*** End Patch'));}

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
